title: A Low-Cost Decision Model on CPU: Optimizing DiffusionGemma with vLLM - Part I
gist: League Labs optimized vLLM so eligible DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B structured decision reads run in one engine step instead of two on Intel AMX CPUs, cutting latency 18.8% on C4, lifting throughput 5.5-15% and lowering monthly replica cost 79% versus an A100. Under sustained load GPUs remain cheaper per decision; decision-stability analysis is deferred to Part II.

insights.claim: League, a healthcare company, wants a self-hosted open-weights decision model like TypeSafe's Jev with low latency, and chose DiffusionGemma (Apache 2.0) because diffusion fills all answer slots in parallel instead of generating tokens one at a time.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: Open-weights, self-hostable decision models are being built as alternatives to hosted services, especially in regulated healthcare.

insights.claim: DiffusionGemma 26B-A4B in BF16 needs 48.1 GiB, which exceeds two 24GB L4 GPUs and forces an 80GB A100 costing $4,754 per month for one always-on Vertex AI replica.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: Model size relative to cheap-GPU memory is what pushes bursty workloads toward CPUs.

insights.claim: A 24-vCPU Intel C4 node with AMX runs the BF16 model for about $996 per month, roughly a fifth of an A100, and lowers monthly replica cost by 44% versus C3 and 79% versus the A100.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: For low-traffic bursty services, idle replica cost dominates, so cheap CPU instances beat GPUs on total cost.

insights.claim: GPU quota and availability constrained what League could deploy and when, which was a second motive for evaluating CPU serving.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: GPU scarcity pushes enterprises toward CPU inference when the model is a fit.

insights.claim: vLLM executes every eligible structured read of DiffusionGemma in two engine steps because the canvas is routed through the speculative-decoding data path, a dependency the read does not actually have.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: A pure software-path inefficiency, fixable without changing the model or hardware.
insights.quote: The split comes from the data path, not from a dependency in the read itself.

insights.claim: The single_pass_reads flag fuses the canvas into the final prompt chunk so a read finishes in one engine step, keeping the prompt causal and the canvas bidirectional; it is proposed upstream as vllm-project/vllm#61480, opt-in and CPU-only.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: Upstream-bound open-source optimization; track whether it merges and extends to GPU.
insights.locator: 3.2 Executing eligible reads in one engine step

insights.claim: Three CPU fixes for structured reads (narrow canvases, an int32 versus bool causal mask crash, and async output buffer overwrites) were merged upstream and shipped in vLLM v0.32.0.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: Shows CPU diffusion-model serving is becoming a supported path in mainstream vLLM.
insights.locator: 2.4 Making structured reads run on CPU

insights.claim: On 231 JevBench items the baseline took 462 engine steps and the flag-on build 231, and each removed step saved 0.12 to 0.17 seconds, which is 21-25% of a 188-token read but only 12-13% of a 1,250-token read.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: Savings are a fixed per-step cost, so short-prompt decision workloads benefit most.

insights.claim: The authors infer the extra step is costly because on a CPU every forward pass pays memory-bandwidth cost to read model weights, and each canvas token activates 8 of 128 experts per MoE layer, touching many experts.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: Reasoned inference not directly tested; implies small-token passes are bandwidth-bound on CPUs.

insights.claim: On C4 the optimization cut concurrency-1 latency by 18.8% (95% CI 18.5-19.0%) and 21.2% on C3, moving median decision latency from about 660 ms to about 540 ms on C4.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: Meets sub-second interactive requirements for agents making decisions while a user waits.

insights.claim: The optimization lets every prompt format meet League's under-1-second p95 target, and requests slower than 1 second on C4 fell from 80 of 4,320 to 9, whereas the baseline missed it at 1,059 ms for the conditional-question format.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: Crossing a latency SLO is what makes CPU serving production-viable.

insights.claim: Throughput gains are largest at low concurrency (15% on C4 at concurrency 2) and shrink to 5.5-9% from concurrency 5 to 20 as the machine saturates, with no throughput growth beyond concurrency 15.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: The optimization helps most for sparse bursty traffic, the target use case, not saturated serving.

insights.claim: The 44-vCPU C3 pulls ahead of the 24-vCPU C4 on throughput from concurrency 5 onward, while C4 is slightly better at concurrency 2 and 3.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: More vCPUs only pay off when load is high enough, favoring the cheaper C4 for light traffic.

insights.claim: A repeat baseline run differed by only -0.2%, and the flag-off optimization build was 0.5% slower than baseline, which attributes the speedup to single_pass_reads rather than the prompt-logprob changes or run noise.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: Controls support that the benchmark result is attributable to the flag.

insights.claim: At 100,000 decisions a month a continuously running replica costs $9.96 per 1,000 decisions on C4, $16.74 on two L4s, $17.93 on C3 and $47.54 on an A100, and idle time makes C4 about 13 times costlier per decision at 1 million decisions a month than at full load ($0.078 per 1,000).
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: For bursty traffic the cheapest machine to keep running wins, favoring CPUs; utilization is the key cost variable.

insights.claim: Under sustained load GPUs are cheaper per decision: at concurrency 10, two L4s cost $0.027 and an A100 $0.046 per 1,000 decisions versus $0.088 on optimized C4, although the GPU runs are not like-for-like (FP8, shorter context, earlier vLLM nightly).
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: CPU serving is not a general GPU replacement; when traffic exceeds one C4 replica, GPUs are likely better.
insights.quote: When traffic grows beyond what one C4 replica can serve, a GPU is likely the better choice.

insights.claim: On 231 JevBench items the flag-on build changed 2 decisions on C4 and 4 on C3 with no statistically significant accuracy change, while moving the same baseline from C3 to C4 changed 10, so hardware moved decisions more than the optimization did.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: BF16 numerical differences across batch shapes and hardware alter individual outputs, so decision-model deployments need regression checks when infrastructure changes.
insights.locator: 6. Faster and cheaper, but are the decisions the same?

insights.claim: Part II of the series will examine how batching, hardware and numerical precision (including FP32 repeats) change decisions and how readiness to deploy was judged.
insights.speaker: Mia Ojeda
insights.so_what: Watch Part II for evidence on reproducibility of decision models across hardware.
insights.locator: 6. Faster and cheaper, but are the decisions the same?
